# Statistical Graphs {#sec-graphs-statistical}

The graphs in this chapter are available from the `r keys("Statistical")` button in the **Graphs** section of the **Analyses** tab.
Along with the options described here, each graph's editor includes the [shared pages](#sec-editor-common) (e.g., **Axes**, **Legend**, and **Placement**).

## Histogram {#sec-histogram-dlg}

A histogram shows how the values of a measurement are distributed by sorting them into bins and counting how many fall into each one.
The dataset should have one row per observation, holding the measurement and (optionally) the group that the observation belongs to.

### Variables {-}

**Continuous**: The measurement whose distribution is shown.
Its values are sorted into bins, and the bars show how many fall into each one.

**Grouping** (optional): Splits each bar into stacked segments, one per unique value (e.g., the proportion of each gender within a bin).

### Binning {-}

:::: {.optionssection data-latex=""}
::: {.optionssectiontitle data-latex=""}
Binning method
:::

**Unique values**: Each unique value gets its own bin.

**By range**: Values are sorted into ranges.
The bin sizes and ranges keep the values' floating-point precision.

**By integer range**: Values are sorted into ranges, where the bin sizes and ranges are integers.
This is the most common way of binning.
::::

:::: {.optionssection data-latex=""}
::: {.optionssectiontitle data-latex=""}
Rounding
:::

Select how floating-point values are rounded when being sorted into bins:

**Round**: Rounds values up or down, based on their fractional part.

**Round down**: Rounds values down (e.g., 4.3 and 4.9 are both sorted as 4).

**Round up**: Rounds values up (e.g., 4.1 and 4.9 are both sorted as 5).

**No rounding**: Values are sorted exactly as they are.
::::

:::: {.optionssection data-latex=""}
::: {.optionssectiontitle data-latex=""}
Interval display
:::

**Cutpoints**: Places the bars between the axis lines, so that the ranges of the bins are shown on the sides of the bars.

**Midpoints**: Places the bars on top of the axis lines, so that the bin's range (for integer ranges) or its midpoint is shown beneath the bar.
::::

**Bin labels**: Select the label shown on each bar:

- **Value**: The number of items in the bin.
- **Percentage**: The percentage of items in the bin.
- **Value & percentage**: Both the number and percentage of items in the bin.
- **No labels**: Labels are not shown.
- **Name**, **Name & value**, **Name & percentage**: The bin's name, optionally with its number or percentage of items.

**Show full range of values**: Check this option to include a place on the axis for every bin, even ones without any items.
Unchecking this will put all the bars together, but the axis may have uneven steps.
This only applies when binning by unique values.

**Use neat intervals**: Check this option to round the bins' ranges to multiples of 5, 10, etc.
This only applies when binning by integer range.

**Suggested bin count (0 = auto)**: Enter the number of bins to create when binning by ranges.
Enter 0 to have the program select the bin count.

**Maximum bin count (0 = default)**: Enter the maximum number of bins.
If binning by unique values and there are more unique values than this, then the values will be binned by range instead.

**Start first bin at**: Enter the value that the first bin starts at.
If no values fall into this bin, then an empty slot for it is still included, so that the axis begins at the requested value.

### Showcasing {-}

Showcasing draws attention to specific bins by making the other bins translucent (i.e., "ghosted").

**Ghost opacity**: Enter the opacity of the bins that are not showcased.
A value of 0 is fully transparent, whereas 255 is fully opaque.

**Hide labels on non-showcased bars**: Check this option to remove the labels from the ghosted bars.

**Showcase bins**: Add the bins to showcase.

\newpage

## Box Plot {#sec-box-plot-dlg}

A box plot shows the spread of a measurement, including its median, quartiles, and outliers.
It can show a single box or one box per group.
The dataset should have one row per observation, holding the measurement and (optionally) the group that the observation belongs to.

### Variables {-}

**Continuous**: The measurement whose distribution is shown (e.g., test scores).

**Group** (optional): Splits the measurements into separate boxes, one per unique value.
Without it, a single box is shown.

### Options {-}

**Box effect**: Select how the boxes are drawn:

- **Solid**: A solid color.
- **Glassy**: A glass effect.
- **Fade from Bottom to Top**: A color gradient, from the bottom to the top (or left to right).
- **Fade from Top to Bottom**: A color gradient, from the top to the bottom (or right to left).
- **Stipple Image**: Filled with a repeating image.
  Click `r keys("Images...")` to select the image.
- **Stipple Shape**: Filled with a repeating shape.
  Click `r keys("Shape...")` to select the shape.
- **Watercolor**: The box is warped and looks like it was filled in with watercolor paint (or a marker).
- **Thick Watercolor**: The same as **Watercolor**, but with a second coat of paint, making it appear thicker.
- **Common Image**: A portion of a larger image, shared by all the boxes.
  Click `r keys("Images...")` to select the image.
- **Image**: An image scaled down to fit the box.
  Click `r keys("Images...")` to select the images.
- **Marker**: A felt-marker look, where the outline is rough and slightly uneven and the interior is filled with diagonal hatching.
- **Pencil**: A hand-drawn look, where the outline is a wobbly pencil line and the interior is filled with dense diagonal hatching.

**Show all points**: Check this option to show all the data points on the boxes and whiskers.
If unchecked, then only the outliers are shown.

**Show labels**: Check this option to show labels on the middle points, the upper and lower quartiles, and the whiskers.

**Show midpoint connection**: Check this option to draw a line connecting the middle points of each box.
This only applies to plots with multiple boxes.

\newpage

## Stem-and-Leaf Plot {#sec-stem-and-leaf-dlg}

A stem-and-leaf plot shows the distribution of a measurement while keeping every individual value.
It can also compare two groups back to back.
The dataset should have one row per observation, holding the value and (optionally) which of two groups the observation belongs to.

### Variables {-}

**Continuous**: The values to display.
Each one is split into a stem and a leaf.

**Grouping** (optional): Compares two groups side by side on a shared stem.
This column must have exactly two unique values.

\newpage

## Heat Map {#sec-heat-map-dlg}

A heat map shows a measurement as a grid of colored cells, so that high and low values stand out.
The cells can be shown as one block or as one row per group.
The dataset should have one row per cell, holding the measurement and (optionally) the group whose row the cell belongs to.

### Variables {-}

**Continuous**: The measurement that is color mapped.
Each row becomes one cell, colored by its value.

**Group** (optional): Arranges the cells into a separate row for each unique value (e.g., one row per student).

### Options {-}

These options only apply when a group is used.

**Group column count**: Enter the number of columns to split the groups' rows into (1–5).

**Show group headers**: Check this option to show a header above each column.

**Group header prefix**: Enter the text shown at the start of each column's header.

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
For the color scheme, the first colors are mapped to the lower values and the last colors are mapped to the higher values.
A missing measurement is shown as a transparent cell with a red X in the middle.
:::

\newpage

## Matrix Heat Map {#sec-matrix-heat-map-dlg}

A matrix heat map counts how often each pairing of two variables occurs.
It shows the counts as a grid of colored cells so that the most common pairings stand out.
For example, it can show which high schools send the most students to which colleges.
The dataset should have one row per observation, holding its row and column values and (optionally) the groups that those values belong to.
The order of the rows does not matter.

### Variables {-}

**Row**: The values shown down the rows (e.g., high schools).
This can be a categorical or numeric column.

**Column**: The values shown across the columns (e.g., colleges).
This can be a categorical or numeric column.

**Row group** (optional): Splits the rows into groups (e.g., public and private high schools).

**Column group** (optional): Splits the columns into groups (e.g., public and private colleges).

Groups are sorted alphabetically, and the values within each group are sorted alphabetically (or numerically, for numeric columns).
A value is counted separately within each of its groups, so two schools with the same name (one public and one private) are shown as separate rows.

### Options {-}

**Cell values**: Which value each cell shows. The cells are colored by this value.

- **Counts**: How many observations have the pairing.
- **Percent of each row**: The pairing's share of its row.
For example, the percentage of a high school's students who went to each college.
This is useful when the rows differ in size, because a large high school would otherwise darken its whole row.
- **Percent of each column**: The pairing's share of its column.
For example, the percentage of a college's students who came from each high school.
- **Percent of total**: The pairing's share of all observations.

**Show totals**: Adds a total for each row (in a column to the right) and each column (in a row below), along with the grand total.
The totals are always counts and are not colored.
With percentages, they show what each percentage is out of.
For example, with **Percent of each row** selected, a row's total shows how many students its percentages are of.

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
For the color scheme, the first colors are mapped to the lower values and the last colors are mapped to the higher values.
Pairings that never occur are shown as empty cells.
An observation missing its row or column value is not counted, but its other value is still shown.
For example, a high school whose students have no college listed is shown as a row of empty cells.
An observation missing a group is placed into an unlabeled group, shown after the other groups.
:::

\newpage

## Scatter Plot {#sec-scatter-plot-dlg}

A scatter plot shows the relationship between two measurements, with one point per observation.
An optional regression line can be drawn for each group.
The dataset should have one row per observation, holding its X value, its Y value, and optionally the group that it belongs to.

### Variables {-}

**X (independent)**: The measurement plotted along the x axis (e.g., hours studied).

**Y (dependent)**: The measurement plotted along the y axis (e.g., an exam score).

**Grouping** (optional): Draws a separate series of points, with its own regression line, for each unique value.

### Options {-}

**Show regression lines**: Check this option to draw a regression line for each group.

**Show confidence bands**: Check this option to draw a confidence band around each regression line.

**Confidence level**: Enter the confidence level of the bands (e.g., 0.95).

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
If either the X or Y value is missing, then the point is left out of both the plot and the regression calculation.
:::

\newpage

## Bubble Plot {#sec-bubble-plot-dlg}

A bubble plot is like a scatter plot, but with each point sized by a third measurement.
The dataset should have one row per observation, holding its X value, Y value, and size value, and optionally the group that it belongs to.

### Variables {-}

**X (independent)**: The measurement plotted along the x axis (e.g., a city's population).

**Y (dependent)**: The measurement plotted along the y axis (e.g., an average income).

**Size (area)**: The measurement that controls how large each bubble is.
The bubbles are scaled by area, with the smallest value getting the smallest bubble.

**Grouping** (optional): Draws a separate series of bubbles, with its own regression line, for each unique value.

### Options {-}

**Show regression lines**, **Show confidence bands**, and **Confidence level**: The same as the [**Scatter Plot**](#sec-scatter-plot-dlg) options.

**Min bubble radius**: Enter the radius of the smallest bubble.

**Max bubble radius**: Enter the radius of the largest bubble.

\newpage

## Chernoff Faces Plot {#sec-chernoff-dlg}

A Chernoff faces plot draws each observation as a face, with each variable controlling a facial feature.
Similar observations look alike, and outliers stand out.
The dataset should have one row per face, with a numeric column for each feature to vary.
Values are scaled to the range of their column.

### Variables {-}

Assign a column to each feature that you want to vary.
Features that are not assigned keep their default look, so only assign the variables you want to compare.

- **Face width**: Narrow to wide.
- **Face height**: Short to tall.
- **Eye size**: Small to large.
- **Eye position**: Low to high on the face.
- **Eyebrow slant**: Angled down to angled up.
- **Pupil position**: Looking left to looking right.
- **Nose size**: Small to large.
- **Mouth width**: Narrow to wide.
- **Mouth curvature**: Frown to smile.
- **Face color**: Pale to saturated, within the skin color range.
- **Ear size**: Small to large.
- **Hair style** (categorical): Each category is given its own hair style, in the order that the categories first appear.
  This overrides the **Hair style** selected below.
- **Hair addition** (categorical): Each category is given its own addition (e.g., a beard or mustache on male faces, a flower or star on female faces).

### Appearance {-}

**Gender**: Select whether the faces are drawn as **Female** or **Male**.

**Hair style**: Select the hair style for the faces (e.g., *Comb-over*, *Flat top*, or *Long & curly*).

**Skin color**: Select the two colors that define the range of skin colors.
The **Face color** variable maps its values within this range.

**Eye color**: Select the color of the eyes.

**Hair color**: Select the color of the hair.

**Lipstick color**: Select the color of the lipstick (female faces only).

**Show labels (from ID column)**: Check this option to label each face (beneath it) with the dataset's ID column.

**Use enhanced legend** (on the **Legend** page): Check this option to use a legend that includes a face graphic with its features labeled.

::: {.notesection data-latex=""}
At most 36 faces (a 6 × 6 grid) are drawn, so filter or aggregate larger datasets first.
A missing feature value is drawn as the midpoint of that feature, and a row with every feature missing is not drawn.
:::

\newpage

## Wilmarth Bridge Plot {#sec-wilmarth-bridge-dlg}

A Wilmarth bridge plot shows observations fading out of a study over time as a grid of characters.
The tapering silhouette traces the survival curve.
The dataset should have one row per observation, with the period it entered the study and the period it exited.

### Variables {-}

**Label**: Identifies each observation, which is drawn as one column of cells.
Rows sharing a label are combined into a single observation.

**Entry** (optional): The period that the observation entered the study.
If not provided, then the first period is used.
This must be the same type (number or date) as **Exit**.

**Exit**: The last period that the observation was observed, whether its event occurred or its follow-up simply ended.

**Status** (optional): Whether the exit was an event or a censoring.
A missing value is treated as an event.

**Intermediate event** (optional): Marks an event that happens partway through the study.
Cells from that point on are drawn in a different color.

### Options {-}

**Fade effect**: Select how an observation's ink weakens over its lifetime:

- **None**: Constant ink.
- **Remaining lifetime**: An observation is palest during the period just before it exits the study.
- **Elapsed time**: Every row is fainter than the one above it, so the whole grid washes out from top to bottom.

**Cell display**: Select how each observation's cells are drawn:

- **Labels**: Each cell shows the observation's label.
- **Dots (anonymized)**: Each cell shows a generic dot, which saves space and hides the observations' identities.

**Survival statistics**: Select the survival statistics to show alongside the grid:

- **None**: No statistics are shown.
- **At-risk count**: The number of observations still at risk at each period.
- **Survival percent**: The Kaplan-Meier survival estimate at each period.
- **Both**: Both the at-risk count and the survival percent.

**Terminal row label**: Enter a label to add an extra row after the last observed period, confirming the study's endpoint.
Leave this empty to not include the row.
The row is only drawn if every observation had an event (i.e., none are censored).

**Intermediate event color**: Select the color used for an observation's cells from its intermediate event onward.

**Show censored markers**: Check this option to mark censored observations with an arrow past their final cell.
